gal.c: GAL Ve tical in old Writers, hath the same Signification as Gabel le in French: And for the better understanding of Ancient Records, Statutes, Charters c, yon should know, that Gabel, or Gavel, Gab lum, Gabellum, Gabellettum, Galbellettum, and Gavillettum, do all signify a Rent, Custom, Dury, or Service, yielded or done to the King, or some other Lord: and Dr. Comell seems to have judg'd right, that Gab lum is to be diftinguith'd from a Rent or Payment made, or a Contract or Bargain; and hath only Relation to such a Payment or Service as was imposed by the Power and will of the Lord.:;

gabelendofahonfe.c: GABEL-End of a Honfe, is the Upright Triangular End, from the Cornith or Eaves, to the Top of its Roof.:

gageinjoinery.c: GAGE, in Joinery, is an Instrument made to strike a Line truly parallel to the straight Side of any Board or Piece of Stuff. Its chief Ule is for gaging of Tenants true to fit into Mortis fes, and lor gaging Stuff of an equal Thickness. It is made of an oval piece of Wood, fitted on upon a square Stick, to slide up and down stiffly thereon, and with a Tooth in the End of a Staff, to core or strike a Line upon the Sruff at any Distance, according to the Distance of the Oval from ir.

gaininarchitecture.c: GAIN, in Architecture, is the Workmen's Term for the Bevilling Shoulder of the Joist or other Timber. " Tis used also for the lapping off the End of the Joist, c. upon a Trimmer or Girder; when the Thickness of the Shoulder is cut into the Trimmer alio, and bevilling upwards that it may just receive the Gain; and so the Joist and Trimmer lie even and level with their Surface. This way of working is used in Floors and Hearths.

gainagiumorwainagium.c: GAINAGIUM, or Wainagium, signifies all manner of Plough-Tackle, or Instruments used in Husbandry, without any Respect to Gain, or Profit, For as Magna Charta provides, That the Knight and Freeholder shall be amerced Sa / vo Con tenemento suo, and the Merchant Salva Merc an - dist sun; so the Villain Countryman, or Plowman, was to be fined or amerced for his Offences, bur still Salvo Guinagio suo, i. e. Saving all bis Plow-Geers, and aacitios Implements of Husbandry: For he was not to be fined 0 as to be ruined and undone, by taking from him the necessary Means of Life.

galeasse.c: GALEASSE, isa large low-built heavy Vessel, using Sails and Oars: Ic hath three Masts, and those not to be lowered, as they are in a Galley. They have three Tire of Guns in the Head, and usually two Tire in the Stern. In two Dutch Prints that I have of a Galeasse, there are 25 Oars of a Side; and I'm told, there is about 6 or 7 Men to an Oar.

gallons.c: GALLONS, were formerly the French Ships of War; - but now the Word is only used amongst the Spaniards and Italians. And the Spaniards do now call only those Ships Gale ons, which are sent annually to La Vera Cruse, or other Places, in the Weft-Indies, vo fetch home Bullion.

gallehalpens.c: GALLEHALPENS, were formerly a Genoa As, Coin, brought into England by the Merchants of thar City; who rifling higher in Galleys, lived commonly, in a Lane near Tower-street, call'd from them Galley-Lane; and they landed their Goods at a Place in Thames-street, call'd Galley - Key 5 and they traded with their own mall Silver in, which our People call'd Gallebalpence. Bur these, together with two kinds of Coin, call'd Su skins and Dot kins, were forbidder by the Statute of 3 H. V. 1. See Stow's Survey of London - 137. P GALLERY of a Mine, is any Branch of it carried on towards any Place. For the Besiegers, and the Besieged, do carry each of them Galleries or Branches under Ground, in search of one another's Mines, which often meet and destroy one another.

galley.c: GALLEY, is a low-built Ship, using both Sails and'Oars, Usually they have only a Main - mast and a Fore-mast, which may be struck or lowered at pleasure. " Tis said, their Length is usually about 130 Feet, and their middle Breadth about 18, and the Length of the Oar is about 36 Feet, and about 4 or 5 Mento an Oar. They are of Service only in the Mediterranean, and such still quiet Seas, These were like the Roman Li - burnice. gaming.c: GAMING. For the Laws of Chance in Games. See Play.

garblerofspices.c: GARBLER of Spices, is an Officer of great Antiquity in the City of London, who may enter into any Shop, Warehouse, &c. to view and search Drugs, Spices, &c. and to Garble the same, that is, to make them clean from any Garbles or Dost. See 21 Sac. I.. 19.

garter.c: GARTER. The most Noble Order of the Gamer, is an Order of Knighthood first instituted by our famous King Edward III. 1350. and inferior to none in the World; consisting of 26 Nobles, or Persons of even yet highet Degree 5 i. e. Sovereign Princes, Kings, and Emperors; whereof the King or Queen of England is the Sovereign; and the reft are stile, The Compa - pinions of the Order. See Cambd en, Afbmole, &c.

gaugepoint.c: GAUGE-Point of a solid Measure, is the Diameter of a Circle, whose Area is equal to the olid Content of the same Measure. Thus the So lidity of a Wine Gallon being 231 Cubick Ina ches, ( according to Win chefter Measure;) If you conceive a Circle to contain so many Inches, the Diameter of it will be 17.15; and that will be the Gange. Point of Wine-Measure. And an Ale - Gallon containing 288 Cubick. Inches; by the same Rule, the Gauge-Point of Ale Measure will be found to be 19.15. And after the ame manner may the Gauge - Point of any Foreign Measure be discover'd. And from hence may be deduced, by way of Consequence, that when the Diameter of a Cylinder in Inches is equal to the Gauge-Point of any Measure ( given likewise in Inches;) every Inch, in Length thereof, will contain an Integer of the same Measure, V. gr. In a Cylinder whose Diameter is 17.15 Inches, every Inch in Height contains one entire Gallon in Wine Measure; Hh 2 and D and in another, whose Diameter is 19 - 15, every Inch in Length contains one Ale Gallon.
